title: Iron-Deficiency Anemia in Women
content:
Iron-deficiency anemia is the most common form of anemia, and it disproportionately affects women, largely because of two factors unique to female physiology: menstruation and pregnancy.

Iron is essential for making hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. When the body doesn't have enough iron, it can't produce sufficient hemoglobin, and red blood cells become smaller and paler than normal — a pattern that's often visible in detailed blood test results (sometimes described as "microcytic" anemia) and helps distinguish this type from other anemia causes.

Menstrual blood loss is the leading cause of iron-deficiency anemia in women of reproductive age. Each cycle represents a real, recurring loss of iron, and for most people, dietary iron intake comfortably keeps pace. But for those with heavier-than-typical periods — sometimes clinically termed heavy menstrual bleeding — iron losses can outpace what's replaced through diet, gradually depleting the body's iron stores over months. This is one reason heavy or prolonged periods are worth mentioning to a clinician even if they aren't otherwise bothersome: they're a plausible, treatable contributor to fatigue that's easy to overlook.

Pregnancy is the other major risk period. Blood volume increases substantially during pregnancy, and the growing fetus draws on the parent's iron stores for its own development, so iron needs rise significantly. Estimates suggest a meaningful proportion of pregnant women experience iron-deficiency anemia at some point, which is why iron levels are commonly screened during prenatal care and why iron supplementation is often recommended during pregnancy even without a confirmed deficiency.

Beyond these two, other contributors include a diet that's low in iron-rich or iron-absorbable foods (iron from plant sources is generally absorbed less efficiently than iron from animal sources, though this can be improved by pairing with vitamin C), gastrointestinal conditions that impair iron absorption (such as celiac disease or inflammatory bowel disease), and any other source of chronic blood loss.

Symptoms often develop gradually and can be easy to dismiss, since the body adapts to slowly falling iron stores. Early on there may be no noticeable symptoms at all. As it progresses, common symptoms include fatigue and weakness (often the most prominent complaint), pale skin, dizziness or lightheadedness, cold hands and feet, brittle nails, and sometimes unusual cravings for non-food substances like ice (a phenomenon called pica that's specifically associated with iron deficiency).

Diagnosis typically starts with a complete blood count showing low hemoglobin, followed by iron studies — most notably ferritin, which reflects the body's stored iron and is often the most sensitive early indicator of developing deficiency, sometimes dropping before hemoglobin itself falls out of range.

Treatment is usually straightforward once diagnosed: oral iron supplementation, along with addressing whatever is driving the iron loss (for example, evaluating and treating heavy periods). It commonly takes a few weeks of supplementation to see hemoglobin improve, and clinicians often recommend continuing iron for several months afterward to fully rebuild the body's iron stores, not just normalize the blood count. This is general information, not a treatment plan — iron supplementation isn't appropriate for everyone (it can be harmful in certain iron-overload conditions), so testing and clinician guidance should come before starting supplements, not after.
